narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 51.1% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is just over 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. You placed in the second decile, noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were accepted. This signal of academic standing in law school carried more weight than any other piece of information.

Your undergraduate GPA and LSAT score were the next two most important factors, and both worked in your favor. Your GPA of 3.30 is slightly above the average of accepted students, and your LSAT of 36 sits very close to their average of 37.2. These strengths pulled the prediction back toward passing, but not enough to overcome the impact of your third-year class rank.

Your family income and plans to attend full-time were considered but had far less influence on the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance in the remaining years of law school so that your graduating class rank moves closer to the middle of the class or higher. Strengthening that single factor would likely change the model’s prediction and open future application opportunities.
